evidence.paraphrase: Pārvatī asks her father who practiced the vow, who taught whom and what results followed. She praises the questioner, speaker and listener of Gaṇeśa stories as gaining piety and a fruitful life, birth, knowledge and action. Himavat announces an ancient history: at Kailāsa, Skanda bows and praises his father Śiva, who sits among gods, Gandharvas and sages, then prepares to question him.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Skanda asks for a vow through which Varada’s favour places siddhis at hand. Śiva calls it Vināyaka’s favourite, yielding the four goals, increasing sons and grandsons, quickly subduing a king, prince or minister, removing great and minor sins amassed over births and making its practitioner a vessel of siddhis. Verse 14 expressly praises attainment without yajña, dāna, japa or homa; the subsequent teaching nevertheless prescribes japa, homa and gifts. Skanda asks its month, procedure and previous practitioners.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: On Nabhas bright fourth, bathe and visit the guru. Honour him with foot-water, drinking water, clothing and ornaments, then begin with his permission. Address him as Śrī Gaṇeśa and request the wish-yielding vow. After instruction, go with him to the Gaṅgā bank, a tank or a deity-made pond; bathe with white mustard, sesame paste and dhātrī, finish daily rites and return home. Worship from a clean seat by the guru’s method. Make an earthen image on Śrāvaṇa fourth and worship daily until Bhādra fourth, observing brahmacarya with fasting, one-meal, night-meal or unasked-food alternatives.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The teacher prescribes a caturthakāla havisyānna meal and the printed akṣaraṃ madhuraṃ bhuñjan food clause; their exact interval and food meanings remain unresolved. Mantra classes include six letters, the printed dvi-catur expression, one, ten and twelve letters. Daily niyuta or ayuta japa, a half or further-half expression and one-tenth homa accompany unwearied day-and-night Gaṇeśa meditation. A fourth-DAY or alkali-free interpretation is not supplied without collation.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: On Proṣṭhapada fourth, make a gold image of one pala or the stated successive half alternatives, choosing a peacock OR mouse mount. Prepare a pavilion and grain mound, a gold/silver/copper kalaśa and plate, a cloth pair, five leaves and five gems. Worship the seat, place the image and invoke through root, Vedic or previously stated mantras. Offer seating and waters, jewels, pañcāmṛta and fragrant baths, red clothes and sacred thread, ornaments, scents, rice, incense, lamps and food including vaṭaka, apūpa, laḍḍū, rice and pāyasa. Hand-water, fruit, betel, gold fee, parasol, fan, fly-whisk, ārati, mantra-flowers, hymns and thousand-name praise precede Brahmin honour.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Keep a night vigil with song and dance. After morning bathing and daily rites, worship again and perform homa with varied liquids. Honour the ācārya/guru with cows, land, sesame and gold; give ample fees to other Brahmins. Feed 108 Brahmins, more if able, or 21; give food and pāyasa to poor, blind and needy people, offer fees and receive blessings. Eat silently with friends and kin. Śiva concludes that the taught Varada vow gives enjoyment, liberation and all desired fruits.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva tells Skanda of righteous king Kardama, who rules to the ocean limits and has gods attending his court. When Bhṛgu visits, the king rises, honours him like a guru, seats and feeds him. Kardama asks his former-birth identity and the merit behind his unmatched, untroubled kingdom, divine honour, Kubera-like wealth and desired objects appearing at home. He wants to repeat that meritorious practice.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Bhṛgu uses focused contemplation to recount Kardama’s earlier life as a poor, pure kṣatriya. His work does not support the household, and harsh words from his wife and children drive him into the forest without consulting them. He finds Saubhari teaching distress-removing knowledge to disciples among sages, bows, and is welcomed and seated. He asks relief from the verbal wounds of family and friends, heat, cold, hunger and thirst, while admitting he has not become detached from his harsh loved ones.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Compassionate Saubhari considers a remedy and recommends the Varada Gaṇeśa vow, which removes distress and sin and gives the four goals and unsurpassed siddhi. He cites earlier practice by Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and brahmarṣis. The kṣatriya asks Gaṇeśa’s identity, form, nature, acts and origin. Saubhari calls him eternal, stainless, sorrowless knowledge-Brahman, without beginning, middle or end, boundless and all-pervading, the source of Oṃ, Vedas and the world.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Saubhari cites Brahmā’s full hundred years of arduous tapas for creation. Brahmā worships the pleased deity with varied services, divine gems and fruits, and gives the two mentally created maidens Siddhi and Buddhi. Gaṇeśa grants the one-syllable vidyā; the booned Brahmā then creates the world. Viṣṇu previously pleased the deity with the six-letter mantra, made an image and practiced the stated vow and rules without defect for one year. He received a boon and preserved the world. Saubhari urges the kṣatriya to worship this universal cause and leave distress.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The kṣatriya asks the time and procedure, promising practice for relief. Saubhari prescribes Śrāvaṇa’s non-dark fourth through Bhādra fourth, daily sixteen-service worship of an earthen image and Brahmin feeding, promising all wishes. Bhṛgu says Kardama’s former self performs it at Saubhari’s hermitage. At completion, Gaṇeśa’s favour transforms his home into a divine household with servants, cattle and Vedic sound; his adorned wife and children await him. After leaving the teacher he does not recognize the grand house and searches for his former home, until his wife’s messengers bring him in. He recognizes Varada’s power. Bhṛgu attributes his present kingship to the vow.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Kardama joyfully repeats Bhṛgu’s prescribed practice, gains knowledge and dispassion, enjoys desired pleasures, places his sons in his office and reaches Gaṇeśa’s abode without return. Śiva urges Skanda to practice and cites Damayantī, Nala, Candraṅgada, gods, asuras, Gandharvas, sages and people as previous practitioners who gained wishes and a divine destination. Himavat closes his embedded history, promises Pārvatī that the vow will obtain Śiva, and explicitly commands her not to publicize it.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Pārvatī asks why Nala performed the vow. Himavat describes Niṣadha’s king as Veda-knowing, brave, generous, wealthy and pure, skilled with chariot, sword, arrows, bow, quiver and armour, and able to travel the three worlds. His innumerable cavalry, elephants, chariots, bowmen and weapon/fire-weapon fighters frighten Indra and direction-lords. His wife Damayantī is beautiful, virtuous and adorned; Brahmā fashioned her from selected essence and gave her the beauty of women in the three worlds. Minister Padmahasta is valiant, intelligent like Bṛhaspati, skilled in policy like Aṅgiras, tall like Meru and deep like the ocean.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: A court with Apsaras dancers, praisers and brahmarṣis receives Gautama. Nala honours and seats him, calling his own birth, kingship, parents, lineage and life fruitful through the visit. Gautama says he wanted to see the king’s wealth, reports praise by Brahmā, Indra, Hari and Śiva, then asks leave. Nala pleads that he stay to remove uncertainty; the sage agrees. The king asks which merit or tapas produced his extraordinary wealth and who he was in a former birth.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gautama says Nala was formerly a poor, pure, knowledgeable kṣatriya in Pippala city beyond Gauṇḍadeśa. Harsh words from his wife, children and friends lead him into the forest at night without consulting them. Wandering among woods, animals and lakes, he finds Kaushika’s hermitage resounding with Vedic recitation and bows. The compassionate sage raises him and blesses him with Gaṇeśa’s auspiciousness. The joyful former self asks for a method granting wishes, ending poverty, and giving enjoyment and liberation. The printed numbering repeats 25; the body is uninterrupted.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Kaushika teaches a month-long Gaṇeśa vow: make a pleasing earthen image, perform the previously stated procedure and daily worship, and hear the story, thereby gaining success. The kṣatriya first asks Gaṇeśa’s identity so he can practice with knowledge. Kaushika describes the ineffable Brahman whose differentiated forms appear in the world, the world’s creator, father, mother and teacher, meditated on by Brahmā, Indra, Śiva and Viṣṇu.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: With Kaushika’s permission the former self returns home and begins the bright Śrāvaṇa-fourth vow, making the taught image. He meditates on Gaṇeśa while standing, speaking, silent, moving, sleeping and eating. The vow gives success and wealth of elephants, chariots, horses, cattle and servants. He donates for divine pleasure and builds a costly Gaṇeśa temple, enjoys pleasures, then dies and is born as Nala in Niṣadha. Gautama attributes Nala’s steady wealth and three-world honour to this and asks leave.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: After Gautama leaves, Nala trusts his account, makes a fine image, practices the vow, hears Gaṇeśa’s story and worships daily with devotion, obtaining all wishes. Himavat concludes that this is Nala’s practice after Gautama’s instruction about his former-birth vow, whose full glory cannot be narrated.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Himavat tells Pārvatī of the vow practiced by Candraṅgada and his wife Indumatī. The king rules Karṇa city in Mālava, knows Vedas and śāstras, sacrifices and gives generously, and has a brilliant court. Verse 3 prints aṇimādiguṇāpeta; its capacity implication is withheld instead of silently changing it to guṇopeta. Indumatī is virtuous, serves her husband and parents-in-law, handles household duties and worships gods and guests. Ministers strongly urge the king to abandon the grievously sinful killing involved in hunting.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Indumatī is explicitly named as the king’s faithful wife and a servant of her parents-in-law. The king proceeds hunting despite the ministers’ appeal against killing. On horseback, he wears blue clothing and headcloth, armguard and finger protection, carrying a small weapon, sword, shield, bow and arrows with his retinue. Killing game and sending it to the city, he is observed by Rākṣasas.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king trembles on seeing huge Rākṣasas described with cave-like mouths, pit-like eyes, open jaws and sky-reaching bodies. The retinue flees; some die and some faint. A cruel Rākṣasī desires the beautiful king, embraces and kisses him. The minister clause bhage kṛtvā in verse 15 remains unresolved; devouring the servants is explicit. The king escapes into a lake unseen by her, but Nāga maidens seize him and take him to their lower-world residence.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The Nāga maidens adorn the king and ask his identity and origin. He identifies himself as Candraṅgada, son of Hemāṅgada, resident of Karṇa in Mālava, who fled the Rākṣasī and was brought here by them. He attributes his survival to the lake and says his hunting people were devoured. The maidens ask him to become their husband and promise pleasures. Addressing them as mothers, he refuses because he observes a one-wife vow; this address does not establish biological parentage.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king teaches the ethics of Somavaṃśa kings: avoid others’ wealth, harm, wives and slander; study, sacrifice, give and protect refugees; avoid forbidden conduct and perform prescribed duties. He distinguishes three-varṇa duties, Brahmin additional officiation duties and hospitality for all. The rejected maidens angrily curse him to separation from his wife and shackle him. The Rākṣasī drinks the lake water and eats aquatic creatures without satisfaction. A surviving messenger reports the king’s submergence to the queen.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The queen hears of the submergence and falls unconscious. Her friends fan and cool her while weeping. Reviving, she beats her breast, head and face and laments her lost husband: where will he eat, sleep and bathe, who will protect subjects and refugees, and where can either find happiness? She sees the directions as empty, throws away ornaments, breaks bangles and faints again. Her grief expresses limited knowledge of his disappearance; the narrator has already described his living captivity.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Pārvatī asks what the people did for the fainting queen. Himavat says the citizens wipe their own tears, address her as mother, urge her to focus on her son, and claim mourning tears burn the dead. They teach impermanence and compare bodily change with replacing clothes. They conjecture that her husband may have attained liberation or heaven and may return, proposing consultation with a sage knowing past and future before further action. Briefly consoled, Indumatī dismisses them, abandons auspicious married marks and wastes away.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: After twelve years of grief Nārada visits. Indumatī tells him of the twelve-year distress; he says her husband is alive somewhere and orders blue headcloth, ear ornaments, forehead kuṅkuma, bangles and maṅgalasūtra. Trusting the truthful sage, she immediately restores these marks, invites Brahmins, honours him and them, gives gifts, sends sugar to every household and orders music. She gives clothing and betel, dismisses the people, then bows to Nārada again.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Indumatī asks where and how her husband lives and how she can see him, offering even difficult vow, gift or tapas. Nārada prescribes Nabhas bright fourth: morning tooth-cleaning, intention and bathing in river, tank or well, white clothes, a beautiful four-armed earthen Gaṇeśa image and steady sixteen-service worship. Food options are ekānna (a single-food option), one meal, or fasting until Bhādra fourth; music, dance and Brahmin feeding accompany a festival according to means. He promises reunion with her living husband held in Pātāla by Nāga maidens and asserts the truth of his account.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: After Nārada leaves, Nabhas arrives. Indumatī makes the earthen image and offers fragrant clothing, flowers, varied foods, fruit, gold, lamps, flower handfuls, circumambulations, bows and hymns. Name-remembrance, meditation, music, dance and Brahmin feeding please the deity. Living on only one pala of milk, she observes the vow from Nabhas bright fourth through Bhādra fourth to regain her long-lost beloved. The printed verse-number errors do not interrupt the read body.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: At the completion of Indumatī’s vow, Gaṇeśa’s favour changes the Nāga maidens’ minds. They release the king, honour him with clothing, ornaments, gems and wealth, give a mind-swift horse and send him away. He emerges from the lake, ties the horse to a tree and bathes. Citizens question him; when he asks after Indumatī and their son, they recognize and embrace him. They report her recent bath, fasting, emaciation and survival by holding to her son. Other citizens announce his return in the city.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Trusted news fills the queen with joy. She sends ministers and troops, decorates the city with flags, wets its streets, prepares assemblies and adorns herself. She gives cows, land and gold to Brahmins and arranges ārati for married women, then approaches the lake with music. Ministers greet, bow to and embrace the king, and sit by his order. He asks everyone’s welfare and honours them with betel and clothing.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king goes to Indumatī’s camp and has a Brahmin rite performed; the printed dvādaśābdadṛśairdvijaiḥ clause remains unresolved in its exact ritual and agent nuance. The secure sequence is auspicious-day recitation, Gaṇeśa worship first, Śaṅkara worship and Brahmin fees. He breaks Śrīphala and approaches the queen, whom he sees as like the Moon’s remaining crescent. No universal twelve-year rite is reconstructed from the clause.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Married young women perform the king’s ārati and shower parched grain and flowers. The couple wipes joyful tears and recounts the pain of separation, receiving consolation. The king mounts a decorated elephant with four bells, flags and parasol, amid foot escorts. A hundred staff-bearers precede him, with fire-weapon fighters, horse and chariot riders and a printed lakh-elephant formation at the sides. Musicians, dancers and praisers lead the procession into the city; no per-side versus combined elephant total is imposed.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Army dust obscures the sun and decorated city. The king honours leading citizens again and gives clothing and betel before they go home. He feeds Brahmins and eats with kin. At night the couple again shares their grief; the royal priest consoles them and they sleep happily. Hearing all that his wife experienced through the Vināyaka vow, Candraṅgada decides to practice it himself and does so with a festival in the next Śrāvaṇa.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: After hearing her father’s history, Pārvatī joyfully performs the Nabhas vow, makes and worships the instructed image, lives on milk alone and meditates on Gaṇeśa. Śiva’s mind becomes restless and he comes to her hermitage. At Gaṇeśa fourth and completion of the vow she sees bull-mounted Hara, rises, bows and worships him. She asks why he left and forgot her, compares a moment of separation with aeons, and explicitly attributes seeing him to her father-taught Varada vow and its favour.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Himavat arrives and places the goddess’s hand in Śiva’s hand. Gods and Gandharvas worship Gaṇeśa and the couple, with divine drums, flowers and praise. Śiva also praises Gaṇeśa, places Pārvatī on his half-body, mounts the bull and returns to Kailāsa; others return to their stations. Brahmā explicitly closes the account Vyāsa asked about and introduces another story whose hearing is said to free all sins and fulfil wishes.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Bhṛgu returns to the Somakānta frame, saying he will continue what Vyāsa heard from Brahmā. Somakānta and then Vyāsa request further Gaṇeśa stories. Brahmā introduces Śūrasena, king of Sahasra city in the middle country: wealthy, generous, sacrificing and protective, skilled in three powers, six political methods, four strategies and four army types, devoted to gods and Brahmins and ruler of the earth. His wife Puṇyaśālinī is righteous and beautiful; her fidelity is compared favourably with Arundhatī and her lack of envy with Anasūyā.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king and court see a bright aerial vimāna with singing and send messengers to inspect it. The gaze of an unnamed leprous royal messenger, a vaiśya’s son, causes it to fall. Messengers report the crash as due to a harmful gaze. Śūrasena and his people go with music and find Indra with gods and meritorious people aboard. Bowing, the king praises the fortune of seeing Indra and asks why the vehicle fell and where he came from and was going.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Indra repeats Nārada’s report of visiting Bhṛśuṇḍi, whose continuous Gaṇeśa meditation and japa have brought Gaṇeśa’s likeness. Nārada was honoured by the sage and came to tell Indra. Indra honoured and dismissed Nārada, then visited the Gaṇeśa-like sage by swift vimāna, exchanging honours. He was returning with his retinue to Amarāvatī when the messenger’s gaze caused the fall near Śūrasena’s city. The king asks which austerity produced the sage’s form.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Indra recounts the former life of the kaivarta Nāmā in Nandura of Daṇḍakāraṇya. A thief from childhood, adulterer in youth, false oath-taker, gambler and drinker, he is expelled from the village. Living with a female companion and child in a forest cave, he kills travellers and animals, grows wealthy, adorns the woman and her son, and sells stolen objects in another city. His ambush weapons include sword, shield, noose, bow, a staff with iron at both ends and full quivers.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Chasing a traveller for a yojana, Nāmā falls, recovers and bathes at a Gaṇeśa tīrtha only to remove fatigue. On returning he sees Mudgala japping the deity’s name-mantra and raises an unsheathed sword to kill him, but even his fastened weapons fall and his mind changes through the devotee’s power. Mudgala laughs and asks why. Indra attributes Nāmā’s knowledge and dispassion to the bath and the sage’s sight. Nāmā confesses countless sins, renounces the weapons and asks rescue from transmigration, saying holy company benefits even wrongdoers.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Compassionate Mudgala remembers the fault of rejecting one seeking refuge. He says Nāmā is not entitled to prescribed gifts and other formal rites, yet offers all-siddhi name-japa. Nāmā bows; the sage teaches Gaṇeśāya namaḥ and plants his own staff before him. He commands one fixed seat, air diet and one-pointed japa until the sage’s return and the staff’s sprouting, with uninterrupted watering of its root morning and evening. A parenthetic line describes the protective hand placed on the disciple’s head.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Nāmā practices from a fixed seat beneath a tree, without food or desires and with controlled senses, japping the name. After a thousand years the staff sprouts; he continues waiting for the sage while anthill and vines cover him. Mudgala returns by chance, remembers the staff and disciple, sees the sprout and eyes-only ascetic, removes the anthill and sprinkles enchanted water. A divine Gaṇeśa-like body with two hands continues japa. On awakening, fire from the eyes rises to burn the three worlds, but Mudgala stops it. The guru’s return has no additional numerical interval.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The awakened disciple bows to and embraces his compassionate guru like a son embracing his father. Mudgala honours the anthill-reemerged one as son, names him Bhṛśuṇḍi and teaches the one-syllable mantra. Verse43 connects the name with a trunk through the raw clause bhūmadhyān nirgatā śuṇḍā; its exact anatomical meaning is unresolved, and eyebrow-middle is not silently substituted. Mudgala grants excellence among sages, worship by Indra, gods, Gandharvas and Siddhas, Gaṇeśa-like sin-destroying meditation and sight, fame, fruitful sight for visitors and a lifespan of a hundred thousand kalpas by his word. narrative_events.details: Pārvatī asks her father who practiced the vow, who taught whom and what results followed. She praises the questioner, speaker and listener of Gaṇeśa stories as gaining piety and a fruitful life, birth, knowledge and action. Himavat announces an ancient history: at Kailāsa, Skanda bows and praises his father Śiva, who sits among gods, Gandharvas and sages, then prepares to question him.
narrative_events.outcome: Himavat opens an embedded Śiva–Skanda teaching.

narrative_events.details: Skanda asks for a vow through which Varada’s favour places siddhis at hand. Śiva calls it Vināyaka’s favourite, yielding the four goals, increasing sons and grandsons, quickly subduing a king, prince or minister, removing great and minor sins amassed over births and making its practitioner a vessel of siddhis. Verse 14 expressly praises attainment without yajña, dāna, japa or homa; the subsequent teaching nevertheless prescribes japa, homa and gifts. Skanda asks its month, procedure and previous practitioners.
narrative_events.outcome: Vow benefits and the no-ritual praise are stated; Skanda requests the procedure.

narrative_events.details: On Nabhas bright fourth, bathe and visit the guru. Honour him with foot-water, drinking water, clothing and ornaments, then begin with his permission. Address him as Śrī Gaṇeśa and request the wish-yielding vow. After instruction, go with him to the Gaṅgā bank, a tank or a deity-made pond; bathe with white mustard, sesame paste and dhātrī, finish daily rites and return home. Worship from a clean seat by the guru’s method. Make an earthen image on Śrāvaṇa fourth and worship daily until Bhādra fourth, observing brahmacarya with fasting, one-meal, night-meal or unasked-food alternatives.
narrative_events.outcome: Guru permission and instruction, month limits and observance options are prescribed.

narrative_events.details: The teacher prescribes a caturthakāla havisyānna meal and the printed akṣaraṃ madhuraṃ bhuñjan food clause; their exact interval and food meanings remain unresolved. Mantra classes include six letters, the printed dvi-catur expression, one, ten and twelve letters. Daily niyuta or ayuta japa, a half or further-half expression and one-tenth homa accompany unwearied day-and-night Gaṇeśa meditation. A fourth-DAY or alkali-free interpretation is not supplied without collation.
narrative_events.outcome: Raw food and numerical terms are retained; precise meanings remain open.

Prepare a pavilion and grain mound, a gold/silver/copper kalaśa and plate, a cloth pair, five leaves and five gems. Worship the seat, place the image and invoke through root, Vedic or previously stated mantras. Offer seating and waters, jewels, pañcāmṛta and fragrant baths, red clothes and sacred thread, ornaments, scents, rice, incense, lamps and food including vaṭaka, apūpa, laḍḍū, rice and pāyasa. Hand-water, fruit, betel, gold fee, parasol, fan, fly-whisk, ārati, mantra-flowers, hymns and thousand-name praise precede Brahmin honour.
narrative_events.outcome: Gold amount, alternative image mounts and the offering sequence are specified.

narrative_events.details: Keep a night vigil with song and dance. After morning bathing and daily rites, worship again and perform homa with varied liquids. Honour the ācārya/guru with cows, land, sesame and gold; give ample fees to other Brahmins. Feed 108 Brahmins, more if able, or 21; give food and pāyasa to poor, blind and needy people, offer fees and receive blessings. Eat silently with friends and kin. Śiva concludes that the taught Varada vow gives enjoyment, liberation and all desired fruits.
narrative_events.outcome: The procedure ends before the Kardama exemplum; its earlier discrepancy remains open.

narrative_events.details: Śiva tells Skanda of righteous king Kardama, who rules to the ocean limits and has gods attending his court. When Bhṛgu visits, the king rises, honours him like a guru, seats and feeds him. Kardama asks his former-birth identity and the merit behind his unmatched, untroubled kingdom, divine honour, Kubera-like wealth and desired objects appearing at home. He wants to repeat that meritorious practice.
narrative_events.outcome: Kardama asks which past practice caused his kingship and how to repeat it.

narrative_events.cause: Failed livelihood and household rebukes drive the former self into the forest.
narrative_events.details: Bhṛgu uses focused contemplation to recount Kardama’s earlier life as a poor, pure kṣatriya. His work does not support the household, and harsh words from his wife and children drive him into the forest without consulting them. He finds Saubhari teaching distress-removing knowledge to disciples among sages, bows, and is welcomed and seated. He asks relief from the verbal wounds of family and friends, heat, cold, hunger and thirst, while admitting he has not become detached from his harsh loved ones.
narrative_events.outcome: Kardama’s former self asks Saubhari for relief; relatives remain unnamed.

narrative_events.details: Compassionate Saubhari considers a remedy and recommends the Varada Gaṇeśa vow, which removes distress and sin and gives the four goals and unsurpassed siddhi. He cites earlier practice by Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and brahmarṣis. The kṣatriya asks Gaṇeśa’s identity, form, nature, acts and origin. Saubhari calls him eternal, stainless, sorrowless knowledge-Brahman, without beginning, middle or end, boundless and all-pervading, the source of Oṃ, Vedas and the world.
narrative_events.outcome: Saubhari provides the remedy and Gaṇeśa’s doctrinal identity.

narrative_events.details: Saubhari cites Brahmā’s full hundred years of arduous tapas for creation. Brahmā worships the pleased deity with varied services, divine gems and fruits, and gives the two mentally created maidens Siddhi and Buddhi. Gaṇeśa grants the one-syllable vidyā; the booned Brahmā then creates the world. Viṣṇu previously pleased the deity with the six-letter mantra, made an image and practiced the stated vow and rules without defect for one year. He received a boon and preserved the world. Saubhari urges the kṣatriya to worship this universal cause and leave distress.
narrative_events.outcome: Nested divine precedents supply exact austerities, mental-maiden gift and mantra/role grants.

narrative_events.cause: The former self performs Saubhari’s prescribed vow.
narrative_events.details: The kṣatriya asks the time and procedure, promising practice for relief. Saubhari prescribes Śrāvaṇa’s non-dark fourth through Bhādra fourth, daily sixteen-service worship of an earthen image and Brahmin feeding, promising all wishes. Bhṛgu says Kardama’s former self performs it at Saubhari’s hermitage. At completion, Gaṇeśa’s favour transforms his home into a divine household with servants, cattle and Vedic sound; his adorned wife and children await him. After leaving the teacher he does not recognize the grand house and searches for his former home, until his wife’s messengers bring him in. He recognizes Varada’s power. Bhṛgu attributes his present kingship to the vow.
narrative_events.outcome: The past vow transforms his household and is said to cause later kingship.

narrative_events.details: Kardama joyfully repeats Bhṛgu’s prescribed practice, gains knowledge and dispassion, enjoys desired pleasures, places his sons in his office and reaches Gaṇeśa’s abode without return. Śiva urges Skanda to practice and cites Damayantī, Nala, Candraṅgada, gods, asuras, Gandharvas, sages and people as previous practitioners who gained wishes and a divine destination. Himavat closes his embedded history, promises Pārvatī that the vow will obtain Śiva, and explicitly commands her not to publicize it.
narrative_events.outcome: Kardama’s succession and no-return destination close his account; Himavat adds a prospective promise and secrecy command.

narrative_events.details: Pārvatī asks why Nala performed the vow. Himavat describes Niṣadha’s king as Veda-knowing, brave, generous, wealthy and pure, skilled with chariot, sword, arrows, bow, quiver and armour, and able to travel the three worlds. His innumerable cavalry, elephants, chariots, bowmen and weapon/fire-weapon fighters frighten Indra and direction-lords. His wife Damayantī is beautiful, virtuous and adorned; Brahmā fashioned her from selected essence and gave her the beauty of women in the three worlds. Minister Padmahasta is valiant, intelligent like Bṛhaspati, skilled in policy like Aṅgiras, tall like Meru and deep like the ocean.
narrative_events.outcome: The king, wife, minister and capacities are introduced; comparison sages are not teachers.

narrative_events.details: A court with Apsaras dancers, praisers and brahmarṣis receives Gautama. Nala honours and seats him, calling his own birth, kingship, parents, lineage and life fruitful through the visit. Gautama says he wanted to see the king’s wealth, reports praise by Brahmā, Indra, Hari and Śiva, then asks leave. Nala pleads that he stay to remove uncertainty; the sage agrees. The king asks which merit or tapas produced his extraordinary wealth and who he was in a former birth.
narrative_events.outcome: Nala asks Gautama to explain the merit behind his wealth.

narrative_events.cause: Poverty and rebukes prompt departure into the forest.
narrative_events.details: Gautama says Nala was formerly a poor, pure, knowledgeable kṣatriya in Pippala city beyond Gauṇḍadeśa. Harsh words from his wife, children and friends lead him into the forest at night without consulting them. Wandering among woods, animals and lakes, he finds Kaushika’s hermitage resounding with Vedic recitation and bows. The compassionate sage raises him and blesses him with Gaṇeśa’s auspiciousness. The joyful former self asks for a method granting wishes, ending poverty, and giving enjoyment and liberation. The printed numbering repeats 25; the body is uninterrupted.
narrative_events.outcome: Nala’s former self seeks a remedy from Kaushika; duplicate verse numbering leaves no body gap.

narrative_events.details: Kaushika teaches a month-long Gaṇeśa vow: make a pleasing earthen image, perform the previously stated procedure and daily worship, and hear the story, thereby gaining success. The kṣatriya first asks Gaṇeśa’s identity so he can practice with knowledge. Kaushika describes the ineffable Brahman whose differentiated forms appear in the world, the world’s creator, father, mother and teacher, meditated on by Brahmā, Indra, Śiva and Viṣṇu.
narrative_events.outcome: Guru instruction and deity knowledge precede the vow.

narrative_events.cause: The month-long vow is performed with continuing Gaṇeśa remembrance.
narrative_events.details: With Kaushika’s permission the former self returns home and begins the bright Śrāvaṇa-fourth vow, making the taught image. He meditates on Gaṇeśa while standing, speaking, silent, moving, sleeping and eating. The vow gives success and wealth of elephants, chariots, horses, cattle and servants. He donates for divine pleasure and builds a costly Gaṇeśa temple, enjoys pleasures, then dies and is born as Nala in Niṣadha. Gautama attributes Nala’s steady wealth and three-world honour to this and asks leave.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual wealth, donations, temple building, death and Nala’s rebirth are narrated.

narrative_events.details: After Gautama leaves, Nala trusts his account, makes a fine image, practices the vow, hears Gaṇeśa’s story and worships daily with devotion, obtaining all wishes. Himavat concludes that this is Nala’s practice after Gautama’s instruction about his former-birth vow, whose full glory cannot be narrated.
narrative_events.outcome: Nala’s current-life repeated vow fulfils his wishes and closes the account.

narrative_events.details: Himavat tells Pārvatī of the vow practiced by Candraṅgada and his wife Indumatī. The king rules Karṇa city in Mālava, knows Vedas and śāstras, sacrifices and gives generously, and has a brilliant court. Verse 3 prints aṇimādiguṇāpeta; its capacity implication is withheld instead of silently changing it to guṇopeta. Indumatī is virtuous, serves her husband and parents-in-law, handles household duties and worships gods and guests. Ministers strongly urge the king to abandon the grievously sinful killing involved in hunting.
narrative_events.outcome: Royal family and the ministers’ warning are introduced; the capacity word remains unresolved.

narrative_events.cause: The king hunts despite the ministers’ warning.
narrative_events.details: Indumatī is explicitly named as the king’s faithful wife and a servant of her parents-in-law. The king proceeds hunting despite the ministers’ appeal against killing. On horseback, he wears blue clothing and headcloth, armguard and finger protection, carrying a small weapon, sword, shield, bow and arrows with his retinue. Killing game and sending it to the city, he is observed by Rākṣasas.
narrative_events.outcome: The royal hunt proceeds despite the warning and encounters danger.

narrative_events.details: The king trembles on seeing huge Rākṣasas described with cave-like mouths, pit-like eyes, open jaws and sky-reaching bodies. The retinue flees; some die and some faint. A cruel Rākṣasī desires the beautiful king, embraces and kisses him. The minister clause bhage kṛtvā in verse 15 remains unresolved; devouring the servants is explicit. The king escapes into a lake unseen by her, but Nāga maidens seize him and take him to their lower-world residence.
narrative_events.outcome: Escape from the Rākṣasī leads to Nāga captivity; the minister clause remains open.

narrative_events.details: The Nāga maidens adorn the king and ask his identity and origin. He identifies himself as Candraṅgada, son of Hemāṅgada, resident of Karṇa in Mālava, who fled the Rākṣasī and was brought here by them. He attributes his survival to the lake and says his hunting people were devoured. The maidens ask him to become their husband and promise pleasures. Addressing them as mothers, he refuses because he observes a one-wife vow; this address does not establish biological parentage.
narrative_events.outcome: The king identifies his father and refuses marriage through his one-wife vow.

narrative_events.cause: The king’s one-wife refusal provokes the maidens’ curse and captivity.
narrative_events.details: The king teaches the ethics of Somavaṃśa kings: avoid others’ wealth, harm, wives and slander; study, sacrifice, give and protect refugees; avoid forbidden conduct and perform prescribed duties. He distinguishes three-varṇa duties, Brahmin additional officiation duties and hospitality for all. The rejected maidens angrily curse him to separation from his wife and shackle him. The Rākṣasī drinks the lake water and eats aquatic creatures without satisfaction. A surviving messenger reports the king’s submergence to the queen.
narrative_events.outcome: Curse and physical captivity follow refusal; the queen receives only a disappearance report.

narrative_events.details: The queen hears of the submergence and falls unconscious. Her friends fan and cool her while weeping. Reviving, she beats her breast, head and face and laments her lost husband: where will he eat, sleep and bathe, who will protect subjects and refugees, and where can either find happiness? She sees the directions as empty, throws away ornaments, breaks bangles and faints again. Her grief expresses limited knowledge of his disappearance; the narrator has already described his living captivity.
narrative_events.outcome: The grieving queen collapses, prompting citizens’ counsel.

narrative_events.details: Pārvatī asks what the people did for the fainting queen. Himavat says the citizens wipe their own tears, address her as mother, urge her to focus on her son, and claim mourning tears burn the dead. They teach impermanence and compare bodily change with replacing clothes. They conjecture that her husband may have attained liberation or heaven and may return, proposing consultation with a sage knowing past and future before further action. Briefly consoled, Indumatī dismisses them, abandons auspicious married marks and wastes away.
narrative_events.outcome: Citizens offer conjectures and temporary consolation; the queen lacks the captivity facts.

narrative_events.cause: Nārada’s assurance changes the queen’s understanding of her husband’s fate.
narrative_events.details: After twelve years of grief Nārada visits. Indumatī tells him of the twelve-year distress; he says her husband is alive somewhere and orders blue headcloth, ear ornaments, forehead kuṅkuma, bangles and maṅgalasūtra. Trusting the truthful sage, she immediately restores these marks, invites Brahmins, honours him and them, gives gifts, sends sugar to every household and orders music. She gives clothing and betel, dismisses the people, then bows to Nārada again.
narrative_events.outcome: Nārada’s assurance restores married-status marks before actual reunion.

narrative_events.details: Indumatī asks where and how her husband lives and how she can see him, offering even difficult vow, gift or tapas. Nārada prescribes Nabhas bright fourth: morning tooth-cleaning, intention and bathing in river, tank or well, white clothes, a beautiful four-armed earthen Gaṇeśa image and steady sixteen-service worship. Food options are ekānna (a single-food option), one meal, or fasting until Bhādra fourth; music, dance and Brahmin feeding accompany a festival according to means. He promises reunion with her living husband held in Pātāla by Nāga maidens and asserts the truth of his account.
narrative_events.outcome: Nārada discloses the living husband’s captivity and gives a conditional reunion remedy.

narrative_events.cause: The queen follows Nārada’s disclosed remedy.
narrative_events.details: After Nārada leaves, Nabhas arrives. Indumatī makes the earthen image and offers fragrant clothing, flowers, varied foods, fruit, gold, lamps, flower handfuls, circumambulations, bows and hymns. Name-remembrance, meditation, music, dance and Brahmin feeding please the deity. Living on only one pala of milk, she observes the vow from Nabhas bright fourth through Bhādra fourth to regain her long-lost beloved. The printed verse-number errors do not interrupt the read body.
narrative_events.outcome: The queen actually performs the taught vow with a one-pala milk diet.

narrative_events.cause: Completion of the vow brings divine favour and changes the captors’ decision.
narrative_events.details: At the completion of Indumatī’s vow, Gaṇeśa’s favour changes the Nāga maidens’ minds. They release the king, honour him with clothing, ornaments, gems and wealth, give a mind-swift horse and send him away. He emerges from the lake, ties the horse to a tree and bathes. Citizens question him; when he asks after Indumatī and their son, they recognize and embrace him. They report her recent bath, fasting, emaciation and survival by holding to her son. Other citizens announce his return in the city.
narrative_events.outcome: The captors release the king, give transport and wealth; citizens recognize his return.

narrative_events.details: Trusted news fills the queen with joy. She sends ministers and troops, decorates the city with flags, wets its streets, prepares assemblies and adorns herself. She gives cows, land and gold to Brahmins and arranges ārati for married women, then approaches the lake with music. Ministers greet, bow to and embrace the king, and sit by his order. He asks everyone’s welfare and honours them with betel and clothing.
narrative_events.outcome: The city prepares a welcome and the king greets his ministers.

narrative_events.details: The king goes to Indumatī’s camp and has a Brahmin rite performed; the printed dvādaśābdadṛśairdvijaiḥ clause remains unresolved in its exact ritual and agent nuance. The secure sequence is auspicious-day recitation, Gaṇeśa worship first, Śaṅkara worship and Brahmin fees. He breaks Śrīphala and approaches the queen, whom he sees as like the Moon’s remaining crescent. No universal twelve-year rite is reconstructed from the clause.
narrative_events.outcome: The worship sequence is secure; the twelve-year ritual expression remains unresolved.

narrative_events.details: Married young women perform the king’s ārati and shower parched grain and flowers. The couple wipes joyful tears and recounts the pain of separation, receiving consolation. The king mounts a decorated elephant with four bells, flags and parasol, amid foot escorts. A hundred staff-bearers precede him, with fire-weapon fighters, horse and chariot riders and a printed lakh-elephant formation at the sides. Musicians, dancers and praisers lead the procession into the city; no per-side versus combined elephant total is imposed.
narrative_events.outcome: The couple reunites and enters the city in a royal procession.

narrative_events.details: Army dust obscures the sun and decorated city. The king honours leading citizens again and gives clothing and betel before they go home. He feeds Brahmins and eats with kin. At night the couple again shares their grief; the royal priest consoles them and they sleep happily. Hearing all that his wife experienced through the Vināyaka vow, Candraṅgada decides to practice it himself and does so with a festival in the next Śrāvaṇa.
narrative_events.outcome: The household is restored and Candraṅgada subsequently practices the vow.

narrative_events.details: After hearing her father’s history, Pārvatī joyfully performs the Nabhas vow, makes and worships the instructed image, lives on milk alone and meditates on Gaṇeśa. Śiva’s mind becomes restless and he comes to her hermitage. At Gaṇeśa fourth and completion of the vow she sees bull-mounted Hara, rises, bows and worships him. She asks why he left and forgot her, compares a moment of separation with aeons, and explicitly attributes seeing him to her father-taught Varada vow and its favour.
narrative_events.outcome: Pārvatī’s previously promised encounter with Śiva is now actually narrated.

narrative_events.details: Himavat arrives and places the goddess’s hand in Śiva’s hand. Gods and Gandharvas worship Gaṇeśa and the couple, with divine drums, flowers and praise. Śiva also praises Gaṇeśa, places Pārvatī on his half-body, mounts the bull and returns to Kailāsa; others return to their stations. Brahmā explicitly closes the account Vyāsa asked about and introduces another story whose hearing is said to free all sins and fulfil wishes.
narrative_events.outcome: Hand-giving, half-body reunion and Kailāsa return close the frame’s personal goal.

narrative_events.details: Bhṛgu returns to the Somakānta frame, saying he will continue what Vyāsa heard from Brahmā. Somakānta and then Vyāsa request further Gaṇeśa stories. Brahmā introduces Śūrasena, king of Sahasra city in the middle country: wealthy, generous, sacrificing and protective, skilled in three powers, six political methods, four strategies and four army types, devoted to gods and Brahmins and ruler of the earth. His wife Puṇyaśālinī is righteous and beautiful; her fidelity is compared favourably with Arundhatī and her lack of envy with Anasūyā.
narrative_events.outcome: Outer narration and a new named royal household are introduced.

narrative_events.details: The king and court see a bright aerial vimāna with singing and send messengers to inspect it. The gaze of an unnamed leprous royal messenger, a vaiśya’s son, causes it to fall. Messengers report the crash as due to a harmful gaze. Śūrasena and his people go with music and find Indra with gods and meritorious people aboard. Bowing, the king praises the fortune of seeing Indra and asks why the vehicle fell and where he came from and was going.
narrative_events.outcome: The fallen vimāna’s cause prompts the king’s questions.

narrative_events.details: Indra repeats Nārada’s report of visiting Bhṛśuṇḍi, whose continuous Gaṇeśa meditation and japa have brought Gaṇeśa’s likeness. Nārada was honoured by the sage and came to tell Indra. Indra honoured and dismissed Nārada, then visited the Gaṇeśa-like sage by swift vimāna, exchanging honours. He was returning with his retinue to Amarāvatī when the messenger’s gaze caused the fall near Śūrasena’s city. The king asks which austerity produced the sage’s form.
narrative_events.outcome: Indra’s reported journey leads to a question about Bhṛśuṇḍi’s likeness.

narrative_events.details: Indra recounts the former life of the kaivarta Nāmā in Nandura of Daṇḍakāraṇya. A thief from childhood, adulterer in youth, false oath-taker, gambler and drinker, he is expelled from the village. Living with a female companion and child in a forest cave, he kills travellers and animals, grows wealthy, adorns the woman and her son, and sells stolen objects in another city. His ambush weapons include sword, shield, noose, bow, a staff with iron at both ends and full quivers.
narrative_events.outcome: Nāmā’s former life, household and robbery weapons are introduced.

narrative_events.cause: An unintended sacred bath is followed by the devotee encounter.
narrative_events.details: Chasing a traveller for a yojana, Nāmā falls, recovers and bathes at a Gaṇeśa tīrtha only to remove fatigue. On returning he sees Mudgala japping the deity’s name-mantra and raises an unsheathed sword to kill him, but even his fastened weapons fall and his mind changes through the devotee’s power. Mudgala laughs and asks why. Indra attributes Nāmā’s knowledge and dispassion to the bath and the sage’s sight. Nāmā confesses countless sins, renounces the weapons and asks rescue from transmigration, saying holy company benefits even wrongdoers.
narrative_events.outcome: The attack fails, the attacker changes and he explicitly seeks refuge.

narrative_events.details: Compassionate Mudgala remembers the fault of rejecting one seeking refuge. He says Nāmā is not entitled to prescribed gifts and other formal rites, yet offers all-siddhi name-japa. Nāmā bows; the sage teaches Gaṇeśāya namaḥ and plants his own staff before him. He commands one fixed seat, air diet and one-pointed japa until the sage’s return and the staff’s sprouting, with uninterrupted watering of its root morning and evening. A parenthetic line describes the protective hand placed on the disciple’s head.
narrative_events.outcome: Mudgala provides qualified name-japa and precise staff/ascetic instructions.

narrative_events.cause: Long japa, staff sprouting and the guru’s intervention lead to the described transformation.
narrative_events.details: Nāmā practices from a fixed seat beneath a tree, without food or desires and with controlled senses, japping the name. After a thousand years the staff sprouts; he continues waiting for the sage while anthill and vines cover him. Mudgala returns by chance, remembers the staff and disciple, sees the sprout and eyes-only ascetic, removes the anthill and sprinkles enchanted water. A divine Gaṇeśa-like body with two hands continues japa. On awakening, fire from the eyes rises to burn the three worlds, but Mudgala stops it. The guru’s return has no additional numerical interval.
narrative_events.outcome: The staff sprouts, divine likeness appears and the guru stops the threatening eye-fire.

narrative_events.details: The awakened disciple bows to and embraces his compassionate guru like a son embracing his father. Mudgala honours the anthill-reemerged one as son, names him Bhṛśuṇḍi and teaches the one-syllable mantra. Verse43 connects the name with a trunk through the raw clause bhūmadhyān nirgatā śuṇḍā; its exact anatomical meaning is unresolved, and eyebrow-middle is not silently substituted. Mudgala grants excellence among sages, worship by Indra, gods, Gandharvas and Siddhas, Gaṇeśa-like sin-destroying meditation and sight, fame, fruitful sight for visitors and a lifespan of a hundred thousand kalpas by his word. Gods and Nārada’s sages visit, praise the fruitfulness of their birth, learning, parents, tapas and fame, and call him Gaṇanātha. He honours and dismisses them.
narrative_events.outcome: Mudgala gives the new name, ritual-son honour, mantra, lifespan and visitor boons.

narrative_events.details: Bhṛśuṇḍi installs a Gaṇeśa image, sits in lotus posture, japs the one-syllable mantra and worships daily with sixteen services. His hermitage has pools, trees and vines, with predators, prey, mongooses and serpents free from mutual hostility. After another hundred years, Gaṇeśa is pleased and asks why his own likeness continues austerity. He promises sāyujya at life’s end, a site named by the raw expression nāmaleti, siddhis for practitioners, no rebirth through seeing the image, sons to the childless and knowledge to students. Indra concludes the origin account and asks Śūrasena’s next question.
narrative_events.outcome: Installation and further worship receive Gaṇeśa’s personal and site promises, closing the origin arc.

narrative_events.details: Śūrasena asks how Indra’s vimāna can fly and what he should do. Indra says properly transferred merit of one year from a Sankaṣṭa-caturthī-practicing Brahmin or kṣatriya in the city will restart it; ten thousand people cannot otherwise accomplish this. The king asks the vow’s merit, result, procedure, deity and earlier successful practitioner. Indra introduces a history of Kṛtavīrya and Nārada.
narrative_events.outcome: One-year merit transfer is prescribed; actual vimāna recovery remains pending.

narrative_events.cause: Persistent childlessness despite many rituals drives the couple’s forest tapas.
narrative_events.details: Kṛtavīrya is a brave, generous, sacrificing, sense-controlled king with moderate diet and devotion, ruling in the Sahyādri region with uncounted forces, gold vessels and beds, and twelve thousand Brahmins fed in rows. His wife Sugandhā is dutiful and devoted to gods, Brahmins and guests. They remain childless despite gifts, vows, austerities, sacrifices and pilgrimages because of former-birth sin. Entrusting realm, seal, treasury, people and districts to ministers, they practice in the forest wearing bark and skin, eating old leaves and air, becoming visible only by their eyes. Nārada sees them and tells the king’s unnamed father in Pitṛloka that his son may die tomorrow or the day after; an heir would sustain life, lineage and heaven.
narrative_events.outcome: Nārada alerts the father to his childless son’s predicted imminent death.

narrative_events.details: Nārada sees Bhṛśuṇḍi’s parents, sons, wife and daughter(s) upside down in blazing Kumbhīpāka, beaten by Yama’s servants. He tells the sage that Indra and other gods and Kapila’s sages seek his Gaṇeśa-like presence, yet his parents, wife, sons, daughters and servants suffer here through his fault. He calls for ancestral rescue. Bhṛśuṇḍi burns with distress. Verse 23 has dual putrau and verse 26 the broader plural roster; names and additional counts are not invented.
narrative_events.outcome: The explicit family roster and Nārada’s rebuke prompt a rescue.

narrative_events.cause: Bhṛśuṇḍi offers vow-merit through a conditional devotional prayer and water transfer.
narrative_events.details: Bhṛśuṇḍi considers a rescue, offers Sankaṣṭa-caturthī merit, views his absent kin through concentration, meditates on Gaṇeśa and holds water. He prays that, if his vow was performed devotionally, its power quickly rescue the ancestors, then casts the water into Gaṇeśa’s hand. Immediately divine favour gives them divine forms and vimānas. Served by Apsarases, praised by Cāraṇas and sung to by Gandharvas, they reach Gaṇeśa’s station. All other wrongdoers in Kumbhīpāka also go to Gaṇeśa’s abode. Indra attributes their actual good destination to one day’s merit.
narrative_events.outcome: Kin and other hell inmates actually reach Gaṇeśa’s abode through one day’s merit.

narrative_events.details: Indra says Śeṣa cannot count the merit of a lifelong devotional Sankaṣṭa vow, and that its power can restart his vimāna. This remains a prospective remedy in the Śūrasena frame; Bhṛśuṇḍi’s completed rescue is the supporting exemplum.
narrative_events.outcome: The narrative returns to the still-fallen vehicle’s prospective remedy.

narrative_events.details: Śūrasena asks what Kṛtavīrya’s father did after the hell-rescue account. Indra says the distressed father goes to Brahmaloka, bows to Brahmā and asks why his virtuous, generous, sacrificing, god-and-guest-devoted son remains childless despite many attempts. Having transferred the realm to his ministers, the son lives emaciated on air in the forest and may soon die. The father asks a remedy for former-birth sin which he can deliver to his son for lineage growth. Brahmā offers a past-birth account.
narrative_events.outcome: The father asks for a former-sin remedy to take to his son.

narrative_events.details: Brahmā describes Sāma, an antyaja wrongdoer whose sight destroys piety. For wealth he murders twelve peaceful Brahmins, leaves their bodies in a cave and takes their possessions. Returning home on Māgha dark fourth at moonrise, he calls his son Gaṇeśa twice and eats with him after taking no food or water. Verse 13 explicitly says tasyaputro’sau dies that night; verse 14’s saḥ reaches Vaināyaka through the unintentional vow, and verse 16’s remaining merit produces the present Kṛtavīrya. The Sāma-versus-son death and rebirth referent is unresolved. Brahmā predicts sonbirth when sins are destroyed; the father trembles and asks another remedy.
narrative_events.outcome: Unintentional-vow merit and royal rebirth are described with a fundamental referent gap.

narrative_events.details: Sāma murders and robs the twelve Brahmins and returns home at night. At moonrise on Māgha dark fourth, after taking no food or water, he calls his own son Gaṇeśa twice and shares a meal with him. This explicit son-name relationship is separated from the uncertain death and rebirth pronouns in the following verses.
narrative_events.outcome: The firm son-name relationship is extracted apart from the later uncertainty.

narrative_events.details: The father asks how the Brahmin-murder sin can end. Brahmā predicts that the royal son’s proper Sankaṣṭa vow will free him from sin. Asked its month and procedure, he prescribes Māgha dark fourth on Tuesday, with an auspicious muhūrta and Moon, tooth-cleaning, twenty-one baths and daily rites, japa, silence and no food. Slander, evil acts, betel, water drinking, harm and tale-bearing are prohibited. At day’s end bathe with sesame and āmalaka paste, use the one-letter, six-letter or Vedic mantra or Gaṇeśa’s name-japa, and meditate steadily.
narrative_events.outcome: Brahmā gives a prospective remedy and its constraints; no cure or sonbirth is yet enacted.

narrative_events.details: Perform sixteen-service Gaṇeśa worship with varied offerings: modaka, apūpa, śaṣkulī, laḍḍū, vaṭaka, pāyasa, rice, accompaniments, fruit, betel, fees, twenty-one dūrvā, lamps and flowers. At moonrise offer arghya first to the tithi, then Gaṇeśa, then Moon. Bow and request pardon; feed twenty-one Brahmins, or ten or twelve if unable, give fees, hear the story and eat silently. Spend the remaining night with music. A careful year of the vow is said to remove all sins and give an excellent son or another desired object.
narrative_events.outcome: Ordered worship, feeding alternatives and a year-long benefit promise are prescribed.

narrative_events.details: Further promises include removal of distress and hostile-army fear. Japa and fasting at a śamī root until moonrise give desired benefits even to blind, mute, intellectually limited and lame practitioners, and give wife, sons, wealth and kingdom. The annual food schedule is Śrāvaṇa: seven laḍḍū; Nabhasya: curd; Āśvin: fast; Kārtika: milk; Mārgaśīrṣa: no food; Pauṣa: cow urine; Māgha: sesame; Phālguna: ghee and sugar; Caitra: pañcagavya; Vaiśākha: the retained term śatapatrikā; Jyeṣṭha: ghee; Āṣāḍha: honey. The father asks why Aṅgāraka fourth is especially praised.
narrative_events.outcome: An annual food schedule and timed practice lead to the Aṅgāraka question.

narrative_events.details: Brahmā answers the father’s question about Aṅgāraka fourth. In Avantī, learned Bhāradvāja performs agnihotra, teaches pupils and observes rites on a riverbank. Seeing an unnamed Apsaras arouses desire; he falls, and emitted semen enters an earth-hole. A red, hibiscus-coloured boy arises, whom Earth lovingly raises. At seven years he asks his mother why he is red in a human body and who his father is. Earth explicitly says Bhāradvāja’s fallen semen met her, produced him, and she raised him.
narrative_events.outcome: Source-specific semen/earth origin and nurturing mother are explicit; no intercourse with Earth or the Apsaras is narrated.

narrative_events.details: The boy asks to see his father. Earth takes him to Bhāradvāja, bows and presents the son born of his semen and raised by her. With his permission she returns home; the sage rejoices, embraces and smells the boy’s head, places him on his lap, and performs upanayana at an auspicious time. He teaches Vedas/śāstras and a Gaṇeśa mantra, prescribing long observance and promising desired gifts when pleased. The boy sits in lotus posture on Narmadā’s bank, controls senses, meditates Heramba and japs on an air diet, becoming thin.
narrative_events.outcome: Explicit father’s acceptance, initiation and teacher/mantra role precede the boy’s austerity.

narrative_events.details: After one thousand years of severe tapas, Gaṇeśa appears at moonrise on Māgha dark fourth. His arms are described as digbhuja, with divine clothes, forehead moon, varied weapons, trunk/tusk/ears/earrings, many ornaments and immense solar radiance. The boy bows and hymns obstacle removal and creation, lordship of gods/asuras, transcendent attributes and world support/protection. Pleased by tapas, devotion, hymn and courage despite childhood, the deity invites desired boons.
narrative_events.outcome: Exact appearance time and boon invitation; digbhuja kept as the witness term, while later image explicitly has ten arms.

narrative_events.details: Bhauma praises the fruitful sight, birth, knowledge, lineage, Earth and tapas. He requests residence in heaven, drinking nectar with the gods, an auspicious name famous in the three worlds, and that the fourth on which he saw the deity always grant piety, remove all distress and give vow-practitioners their wishes through divine favour.
narrative_events.outcome: Personal heaven/nectar/name requests and distinct festival efficacy request are explicit.

narrative_events.details: Gaṇeśa promises nectar with gods and fame as Maṅgala; Aṅgāraka is explained by redness and Earth-son status. Aṅgāraka-fourth practitioners receive merit equal to a year of Sankaṣṭa observance and unobstructed tasks. The boy will become king in Avantī, and recounting the excellent vow gives all wishes. The deity grants and disappears.
narrative_events.outcome: Requests receive specific response, plus prospective kingship and festival benefit; actual transport follows.

narrative_events.details: Maṅgala devotionally installs a beautiful, trunk-faced ten-armed Gaṇeśa, builds a pleasing temple and names the deity Maṅgalamūrti. The site becomes wish-giving to everyone and liberation-giving through observance, worship and seeing.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual named image/temple installation and site efficacy.

narrative_events.details: Vināyaka sends his Gaṇas in a fine vimāna to bring Bhauma. They bring him in the same body to Gaṇeśa’s vicinity. Narrator states he obtained heaven and nectar with gods, giving Tuesday-associated caturthī its fame. Maṅgalamūrti also becomes called Cintāmaṇi for giving desired objects; the all-obstacle-removing deity is famous west of Pārinera city, now worshipped by Siddhas/Gandharvas at moonrise and granting desired gifts, sons/grandsons and prosperity.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual same-body transport and heaven/nectar attainment close the origin/site arc; named king accession remains only predicted.
